title: Effort as practice
hookLine: the fourth: joyful effort, not strain

lines: A MONK WALKING UNTIL HIS FEET BLEED.
cards: A young monk named Sona walks up and down a path in a forest grove, hour after hour, until his feet split and the path is marked with blood. He is pushing as hard as he knows how, and still his mind won't settle.

Alone, he starts to think about quitting: going home, living as a lay person, spending his family's money on good things. The Buddha hears his thought and comes to him. He doesn't tell Sona to try harder, or to give up.
He asks him a question about music. You may remember Sona from earlier on the path. Today his sore feet open the fourth perfection: effort.

teach.b: Sona, before you left home, were you good at the lute? Yes, he was. When the strings were wound too tight, did it sound right?
No. When they were too slack? No.

teach.h: NOT TOO TIGHT, NOT TOO LOOSE.
teach.b: And tuned evenly, neither too tight nor too loose? Then it played well. In the same way, the Buddha says, effort pushed too hard turns into restlessness, and effort too slack turns into laziness.
So tune your effort evenly. Sona does, and in the story he goes on to reach the goal he walked so hard for. That's the first turn: effort is a tuning, not a maximum.
The second turn comes from the Mahayana. In the list of six perfections a bodhisattva trains in, the fourth has a Sanskrit name, virya: energy, vigor.

The poet-monk Shantideva, in his Way of the Bodhisattva, describes it not as grinding but as delight in what is good, taking pleasure in the wholesome thing. That's why some teachers call it joyful effort.
Strain hates the work. Virya likes it. The third turn is where the effort goes.

The suttas name four right efforts: keep an unhelpful state from arising, let go of one that has arisen, bring up a helpful state that isn't there yet, and keep a helpful one going. All four are small and daily.
None is a heroic all-nighter. So the fourth perfection isn't about doing more. It's doing the good thing gladly, at the right tension, and doing it again tomorrow.

how: Buddhists in the Mahayana schools count energy, virya, as the fourth of the six perfections; teachers in many schools use the Buddha's lute image from the story of Sona to describe balanced effort in meditation and daily life.

o: energy that enjoys the good, tuned neither too tight nor too loose
a steady calm that comes from doing nothing at all
pushing yourself as hard as you can until you break through

games.q: effort as practice: tap the pairs.
p: tuned neither too tight nor too loose
effort as delight in the good

s: in the story, the Buddha tells Sona to try even harder
he asks about the lute instead: effort too tight brings restlessness, too slack brings laziness.
Shantideva describes this perfection as delight in what is good
in his Way of the Bodhisattva, effort is taking pleasure in the wholesome, not grinding.
the four right efforts include keeping a helpful state going
the fourth of them is to maintain a wholesome state that has already arisen.

games.q: you're Sona. you've walked the path until your feet bled, and you're thinking of going home. what do you do?
o: go home and give up the robe.
tune your effort like a lute string.
games.why: the Buddha's lute question turns him around: neither straining nor quitting, but even effort. in the story, it works.

practice: Notice your shoulders and your jaw: if they're tight, that's a string wound a little too far, so let it ease a turn; if you feel heavy and dull, sit a little taller.

Picture one ordinary thing you'll do next, washing a cup or answering a message, done gladly, the way you'd play a song you like. Then come back to the breath, neither forcing it nor letting it go slack.

wordCard.voice: Effort as practice. Virya, the fourth perfection: energy that enjoys the good, tuned like a string, neither too tight nor too loose. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit virya (Pali viriya): energy, vigor; the fourth of the six perfections in the Mahayana list.

carryVoice: Your line: the fourth perfection. Too tight or too loose is a question you can ask anywhere. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Shantideva, The Way of the Bodhisattva

sources.ref: the four right efforts (e.g. Anguttara Nikaya 4.13; Samyutta Nikaya 49)
